### 1.3.4 Doctrinal Legal Constructions and the Reconstruction of Individual Sovereignty

Confronted with the pervasive exploitation of digital affect and an attention economy that undermines human mental integrity, conventional positive legal doctrine—hitherto fixated on tangible physical harms and procedural data privacy violations—appears paralyzed and obsolete (Hildebrandt, 2015). What is required is a radical and comprehensive doctrinal reconstruction, commencing with the mobilization of existing civil law instruments, such as the doctrine of defects of will (*vitiated consent*) in contract law (Article 1320 in conjunction with Article 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*)). Grounded in the principle of good faith (Article 1338(3) of the Indonesian Civil Code) and the prohibition of unlawful acts (Article 1365 of the Indonesian Civil Code), any digital agreement or contract arising from fraud or deceit (*bedrog*), mistake or error (*dwaling*), or undue influence (*misbruik van omstandigheden*) systematically orchestrated by manipulative algorithms must be declared null and void (Calo, 2014). AI developers and technology corporations must not be permitted to shield themselves behind standard form contracts or convoluted End-User License Agreements (EULAs) to evade civil liability for the psychological harms inflicted by their products (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008).

Furthermore, on the international and regional legal stage, cutting-edge regulatory frameworks such as the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act 2024 / Regulation EU 2024/1689) have established a critical benchmark through Articles 5 and 50, which explicitly prohibit the deployment of AI systems that utilize subliminal or manipulative techniques to materially distort an individual's behavior in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause physical or psychological harm (Hildebrandt, 2015). Such regulations must be adopted and expanded by national jurisdictions globally, including in Indonesia through strategic harmonization with the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022) (Farahany, 2023). Affective data—such as emotional recordings, vocal intonation patterns, heart rate metrics monitored via wearable devices, and traces of emotional interactions with synthetic bots—must be unequivocally categorized as "Specific Personal Data" requiring consent that is explicit, fully informed, and uncoerced by any form of algorithmic manipulation (Zuboff, 2019).

Reconstructing individual sovereignty within the attention economy demands a paradigm shift from passive data protection to active cognitive sovereignty (Farahany, 2023). The state must intervene not merely as a market regulator, but as a robust guardian of its citizens' mental integrity (Jonas, 1979). This entails mandating independent algorithmic audits of recommendation systems and synthetic companion models, establishing stringent ethical prohibitions against addictive interface designs (*addictive design prohibition*), and granting citizens the legal right to seek compensation for covert psychological manipulation that impairs their mental health (Calo, 2014).

Ultimately, humanity’s last line of defense amid the onslaught of synthetic empathy and attention capitalism is not more sophisticated artificial intelligence, but a resolute reaffirmation of existential autonomy and human dignity (Buber, 1923; Levinas, 1961). The law must stand resolute as a bulwark declaring that the human inner life, affectionate sentiment, and emotional vulnerability are not raw materials free to be exploited by technology corporations for mere financial gain (Weizenbaum, 1976). Individual sovereignty in the digital age must be reclaimed through decisive regulation, incisive jurisprudence, and a collective critical consciousness that refuses to be commodified in the free market of digital affect (Floridi, 2013).
